utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Anything to raise before we hear the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. I do have a couple of matters of some developments that have just -- we have become aware of. First, we received an e-mail yesterday regarding the debriefing of one witness who has already testified, Witness 130. And in this e-mail, there are some rather interesting information, both -- which I would say is extremely inculpatory in nature, assuming that the information that is being provided by the witness is true, accurate, and complete, which -- and I will reserve my opinion as to that. In any event, it would appear, in light of this new information and in light of the potential appearance of another witness from the United States that it will certainly be necessary for us to ask for a -- for some time to prepare and to research and investigate these matters that are being mentioned in the e-mail with respect to the -- to what Witness 130 has said. We assume and we are hopeful that the Prosecution will, on an expeditious basis, provide us with, not necessarily the transcript, but at least the tape-recorded sessions where this witness is being debriefed and is mentioning all these -- this sort of new information, information which the witness did not provide under oath when he testified. And so, it would appear, at least on face, that Witness 130 committed perjury, at a very minimum, during his direct and cross-examination during the Prosecution's case. So another concern is: We would like to know where is Witness 130, in a sense that is he locked up? Because in the e-mail it would appear that he was an enthusiastic killer, one who killed without any remorse. And we saw him -- his demeanor in court as well. And the gentleman was rather cold in his description of the events. But, one, I think that members of the Defence are concerned that a cold-blooded killer like this individual should not be walking around the streets of the Netherlands for our own safety and for the safety of the Dutch people. Because clearly this individual needs to be locked up, assuming what he says is true. Number two, we would like to know from the Prosecution whether any negotiated deals are in the play. And of course, how is it at this stage of the proceedings, this witness, after he's testified on direct and the Prosecution's case in-chief, all of a sudden has decided to come clean. Was it the Prosecution initiating a further follow-up questioning, which is natural in many instances. Or is it that this witness, for whatever reason, perhaps because he has engaged a lawyer, I don't know, now had found sort of a -- as an alcoholic would say a moment of clarity, where he wants to unburden his soul and come clean because he has found a conscience. Those are the informations we would like to know. If the gentleman is not locked up, we certainly would want the individual locked up while at The Hague for that -- for those reasons. So that's number one. Number two, we would like to know from the Prosecution when, if they know, when they can expect this other witness who is mentioned by Witness 130 to be arriving from the United States. It's our understanding that extradition proceedings may have commenced. Certainly the individual, it would appear, is being deported from the United States. I know that that can take some time, though I am sure that the INS, Immigration and Naturalisation Services in the United States are all too pleased to often get rid of unwanted and unwarranted individuals who are there for no particular reason, other than the fact that they have lied to get their way to the United States. So maybe they have some answers on that. Lastly, there is the issue with respect to the disclosure material from the East Bosnian Corps headquarters. We received it this morning. It probably was put over the weekend in the locker, but we looked at it this morning. There doesn't appear to be a large volume. It's for the month of July. In light of the nature of the indictment and the period that the indictment covers, particularly since there seems to be this historical basis upon which the Prosecution is anchoring its joint criminal enterprise motive, criminal responsibility, we would like to know as soon as possible, perhaps Mr. McCloskey is not prepared at this time, but we would like to know how much more material they have, when can we expect it. It's in B/C/S. Luckily it's all typewritten, which helps us a little bit. But I would venture to say that we're going to need, as I said, a -- some time. And I raise it at this point in time because we have witnesses scheduled for this week. For the following week, the witnesses we have yet to notify, as of today, although we have the list, we know who we want, one of them is supposed to be coming by way of a subpoena. We don't know the status of that -- or at least two of them by way of subpoena. But we would like to know, so at least we can perhaps make some arrangements and make an application to the Court when it would be most appropriate to take this break so we can examine this material and also conduct an investigation. And -- so if we could -- I wanted to go on the record. I want to thank the Prosecutor for bringing this to our attention as early as they were able to do so. However, it does cause us a great deal of concern. And I don't want to keep going on with the Defence case knowing, as I do now, that there is this thunderstorm looming ahead - more like a tornado - and is heading in my direction. I don't want it to be on top of me before I react. So that's why I'm bringing it to the Court's attention at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I hear from Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, to start with the East Bosnia Corps collection, the material we got was the first CD, and it had these -- the July daily combat reports from the Main Staff to the presidency. There's very small sections on the Drina Corps. I haven't had time to look at all of them, but it doesn't appear to -- that it will be of any major significance. The other material will be picked up and brought to the office and will be analysed. As I have said before, the connection with the East Bosnia Corps and our events are -- there are some connections, but we don't expect to see a whole lot, but you never know what these collections come up with. So as we find anything, as counsel knows, we will make every effort to get it to people as soon as possible. But I don't see that as a significant issue right now. Regarding the e-mail that I sent to all counsel and the additional information provided by Witness 130, counsel has some valid points and -- regarding the interest that I think the Court would have in this material. It would -- it's not up for me to bring up the information in the material, so at this time I will not. Though, the Court I think to judge the matter properly would want to know more than Mr. Karnavas has said. But I think we can talk about that and determine, you know, what the Defence feels like it wants to -- and I may be going back to my common law roots in this kind of material and the trier of fact, we have no problem with the Court seeing this at all. And I just want to make sure that the Defence is the one that is approving of how much the Court sees. Some of the information is very significant and is the kind of information that the Defence should be allowed to look at, digest, and incorporate into their interviews and perhaps investigate. But I can't really say much beyond that without you knowing the facts of -- or the rough facts. And I think I need to speak with both Defence counsel, it affects both their clients, so that we can get a good feel for what they are comfortable with providing to the Court at this time. We will have a taped transcript very soon. And that information will be to the Defence very soon in a more formal form. I sent an e-mail, which is pretty rough, based on my remembrances of a very brief interviews on Wednesday, Friday, and a very long interview on Sunday. So some of the other matters Mr. Karnavas brought up are really not matters for this Court or open Court, the security issues. And the witness in the U.S., that's a sensitive issue; I would prefer to talk about that in private session, since the U.S. interests may be involved. And I can speak briefly to that, if you wish. Again, it's hard to speak much about this until you have a better understanding of what we're talking about. And as this material is being digested by the Prosecution at this stage of the case, I believe we would be in a position to offer some of it as rebuttal, but perhaps the bulk of it would be a motion to re-open our case. And this is something that is not unusual, as you probably recall from the Krstic record, a document indicating that Krstic was appointed commander came in, it might have even been in the Prosecution's rebuttal case, but it was very late. And with these ongoing investigations, this sort of thing happens; it's just part of the world we're in in these large cases. But I'm reluctant to say anything more, unless you want me to, and I want to talk to the Defence to make sure that any facts that are mentioned are something they are comfortable with. Because they have several options, one be that this information not be divulged to the Trial Chamber, another is a continuance, another would be them calling him as a witness. I mean, there are several options and we haven't really had time to talk about it yet. So I would just leave it -- well, I will just stop talking at this point to see how we want to go further with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. At this moment it's very difficult for this Bench to make any rulings or decisions on this matter. As I remembered that this witness testified some time at the beginning of this year and he's from Zvornik Brigade is more related to Mr. Jokic's defence. But I'm not quite sure about that, because my memory is not long enough. So I hope that if possible the parties could furnish us with more information concerning with this new development. Then we'll study whether -- what's the approach that we should adopt, whether we re-open the Prosecution's case, whether we arrange it in the rebuttal phase, or whether there's some other way out. It's very difficult for us to do anything at this stage. As for the second issue, of course the Prosecution has the obligation to provide any informations they receive to the Defence, but it depends on the relevancy and probative value of those materials. I think same is true that it will be very difficult for us to make any rulings at this stage. As for the time schedule, I believe that we have a very tight schedule. It will be very difficult for us to change that schedule, unless it's absolutely necessary. If there is anything that the parties would like to Bench to do, I hope you could inform us as soon as possible so that we could take it into consideration in due time. But until then, I believe that we have to continue the proceedings because we have the witnesses waiting on the list. Is that all right? Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, obviously, Your Honour, we will do whatever we're instructed to do. We would like all of the East Bosnian Corps material, all of it. We don't simply want to rely on the Prosecution determining what they think is relevant for our case. We believe that we know our case after three years fairly well. And so if they have a lot of documents, we would like to look at them. Secondly, we can provide the Court with more information. I certainly -- recognising that we're not in a common law system and that we're dealing with professional Judges who make decisions every day, I have absolutely full confidence in the Trial Chamber in looking at the material and determining what, if any, is admissible, relevant to this particular case. I think that when the Court sees it, it will rapidly come to the conclusion that it is extremely relevant to the Blagojevic Defence case and that it is of such magnitude that it will require us some time to get to the bottom of it. Since I'm in my case, I don't want to have to wait to deal with this matter on rebuttal because I don't know what they want to do and I don't care what they want to do. I know what I want to do and I want to deal with that in my case. So since I have this material, I want to be able to take the wind out of the sail, as the term is, but as opposed to them getting another shot at re-opening their case. They've had seven years to nine years to get their story straight. They've had this gentleman well in their hands, in their grasp, in their reach. They brought him on, they put him on and now, for whatever reason, he's singing a different tune. How and why and under what circumstances, that's something we need to know. I'm going to be dealing with this in my case in-chief, so we all know right up front. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may ask the Trial Chamber to move into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I apologise to you for having kept you waiting for a long time, because we have some technical issues to discuss and to deal with. And now are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I didn't hear you, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Mile Janjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your last name letter by letter.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: J-a-n-j-i-c.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Janjic, July 1995, were you a member of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us what position you held within the Bratunac Brigade back in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the military police platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's stay with July 1995, and I'm going to give you two days, two dates, as reference points. July 6th, being the day when the events commenced against Srebrenica, July 11th, 1995, the day Srebrenica fell. Sir, could you please tell us prior to July 6, were you aware of any activities that were about to begin against Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us prior to that date if you recall what you were doing.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I was involved in my regular police work within my everyday activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where you were immediately prior to July 6th?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I was at the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, were you stationed in Bratunac? Is that where you were working, in Bratunac town, or had you been assigned to any places to guard?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: For the most part, it involved work in Bratunac and going out into the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now -- and where would you go out into the field?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, we were engaged in providing security along the Sase/Pribicevac road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What sort of shifts would you have when you were out there doing that kind of fieldwork?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: For the most part, we went in groups. We provided security during the day; in the evening, we would go back and we would be free.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I won't be using the ELMO. Is there any way we can lower it? There seems to be some obstruction -- there you go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry for that interruption. Now, on July 6th, 1995, do you recall where you were on that particular day, the day that the events commenced against Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't recall the exact date, but five, six, or seven days before that I was engaged in various periods in this security detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did anything unusual happen or were you involved in anything unusual from July 6th to July 11th, 1995, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's focus on July 11th. That would be the day that Srebrenica fell. Do you recall on that particular day where you were?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: On that day, I was also providing security along the Sase/Pribicevac road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do that for the entire day?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether you stayed over there overnight or did you come in to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No. That was done until late in the afternoon, and afterwards we would return to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you would return to Bratunac, would you check in with the Bratunac Brigade military police? Would that be one of the formalities?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Then, before that, after that, always.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall whether you checked in to the Bratunac Brigade military police on that particular day when you came back into Bratunac from guarding the road at Sase, at the Sase mine?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether on that particular day when you did report, whether you received any additional instructions or tasks to perform?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what tasks you received and from whom?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, late in the afternoon just before dark, we were gathered in front of the military police building by Momir Nikolic. He ordered us to use the military police insignia, to put them on our arms, to take our personal weapons, and to go to the Fontana Hotel in Bratunac. And that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you say "insignia," could you please tell us so we all know exactly what you are speaking about, insignia for -- that would designate you as a military police officer.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, it's the insignia we used otherwise when we were engaged in activities, when we were engaged in this kind of police work. These are emblems that were worn on the upper arm, below the shoulder that is. The name of the unit was on that emblem and the army, things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also have a white belt with a little stripe that goes on that we sometimes see?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We did not have the little stripe. I know what you are referring to, but belts we did have, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you go to the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. We went on foot in the direction of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you please tell us when you went to Hotel Fontana to whom you reported, if anyone.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: In front of the hotel we were met by men who introduced themselves as the personal security detail of General Mladic. And they gave us these certain tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what tasks you were given.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We were asked to provide this broader security around the Fontana Hotel, to stop traffic in the street that passes in front of the Fontana Hotel, to keep all civilians away, all persons who happened to be in front of the building at that moment, that is what we were asked to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, was that -- was part of your duties just to protect the exterior of the Hotel Fontana, or did that include the interior as well?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: At that moment, only the exterior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did that change at some point, in other words, to include the interior as well?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you please tell us about what time would it have been when you were also tasked to guard the interior as well.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact time frame, but it was after some negotiations that were held on the ground floor of the Fontana Hotel. When these negotiations were over, these young men told us to provide security for the rooms upstairs as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we speak about what you did that evening, could you please tell us how many members of the Bratunac Brigade military police had been tasked to go to Hotel Fontana on the evening of July 11th to provide security.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly, but it could have been 10 to 15 policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Were there others guarding the Hotel Fontana as well, other than the Bratunac Brigade military police?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a komandir, a commanding officer, among you, someone who had been designated by Momir Nikolic to be in charge of the members of the Bratunac Brigade while on that assignment?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell us where did you -- eventually you said that at some point you were guarding the interior as well. What portions of the inside of Hotel Fontana were you guarding, you and your fellow MPs?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: That evening we were involved in security upstairs as well in the hotel, as I already said. We worked in shifts consisting of two men at the very beginning of the stairs, so to speak, not to allow anyone to pass there or to go upstairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please tell us for how long you were at the Hotel Fontana when you were tasked to go there and provide security.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: All night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what point then did you leave, if you recall, that area?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It was early in the morning. I cannot remember the exact time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us who, if anyone, issued the order for you and the other members of the Bratunac Brigade military police to leave your posts?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, meaning there was no one?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We went along with the orders given to us the previous evening, to provide security at the hotel during the night, to spend the night there, and then to report at the military police platoon on the following day. So it was only the night that was referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And where did you and the other members of the military police go after you left the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We went to the military police building within the framework of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would you recall what time that would have been? Are you able to recall?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As I said, early in the morning. I cannot recall the exact time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you got there did you receive any orders?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you there? How long were you there that morning?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, perhaps an hour, an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And after that what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, we came there. When we reported at the military police platoon, we found Mirko Jankovic there and his deputy Mile Petrovic. They told us not to go anywhere, to wait, that Momir said that we should be on the ready. Where he was and where we would be going is something they did not tell us. We sat there at the military police premises. We had breakfast, and we were waiting. After a while, one of the two, I can't remember who exactly, walked in to the room and said that Momir had called from Zuti Most and that the military police platoon should go to Zuti Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, first of all just for the record, who is Mirko Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The commanding officer of the military police platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. From the Bratunac Brigade headquarters to the Zuti Most, what's the distance?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, perhaps about 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, when -- so did you wait for Momir Nikolic to return?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No. He asked us to go to Zuti Most and he said that he would be waiting for us up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you go to Zuti Most?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, the first group, including myself, took the military vehicle that we had for our own use, that was a TAM truck, and we headed in the direction of Zuti Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you dressed at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. He told us to take those emblems of the military police, to make sure we did that, and also to take our personal weapons. He didn't ask for anything special.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say "he," who are we speaking about, Mirko Jankovic or Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Mirko Jankovic told us all of this, but he said that it was Momir Nikolic who asked for all of those things to be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how many members of the military police went with you to the Zuti Most that morning?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. I didn't count. 10 to 15 maybe, merely a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the vehicle you were travelling in, were all members of the military police that were scheduled to go from the Bratunac Brigade headquarters to the Zuti Most, could they all fit in, in that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how many trips were made or how many vehicles were used to transport the members of the military police there?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We were brought to the Zuti Most, where it gets broader. 20 minutes -- 20 metres from the bridge on the left side there is a clearing, and that's where we were left. And the vehicle then went back to Bratunac to pick up the other members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given any instructions when you arrived in Zuti Most?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: When we got out of the vehicle, Momir Nikolic in person came up to us. He said: "Move on forward. I will catch up with you. And move ahead, and I will be waiting for you up there."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which direction would you have been moving forward to?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: In the direction of Potocari, in the direction of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, from the place where you were left off, some 20 metres past the Zuti Most where there is a larger area in the road, could you see ahead of you? Could you see whether there were -- whether there was a mass of people?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No. Because the layout of the terrain is such that -- it's a winding road. All you can see ahead is 50, 100 metres maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than being told by -- or ordered I should say, by Momir Nikolic to move ahead, at that point in time did you receive any other orders?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know by any chance, be it by rumour or otherwise, what you were going to be tasked to do for that day?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you move forward, as ordered by Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at some point in time did Momir Nikolic -- did you catch up with Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No, he caught up with us and moved ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now -- so he was ahead of you as you were going forward. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, he moved ahead, as I said, in his car and we couldn't see him anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you see him again later on?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what point? Where was he when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We were moving in the direction of Potocari, and at a point facing the concrete factory or the battery-producing factory he approached at one point. And we -- we met, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much time had lapsed from the time that you saw him where he said to move ahead, to the time when you met up with him again?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It's a distance of about a kilometre. It could take 10 minutes, maybe, if you move quickly on foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you met up with him again by the concrete factory or the battery-producing factory, were you given any instructions by Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you tell us what instructions you were given, could you please tell us how many members of the Bratunac Brigade military police were with you at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: At that time, that first group including me was there. So we were 10 or 15 maybe. We came there first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us: What orders did you receive from Momir Nikolic at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: At that moment -- I suppose there was more than one order; I heard two. The first was when he spoke to us that he would require a Pinzgauer vehicle to be brought in, which is something like a combat vehicle, that it would have a specific task. He will say what and when. And then he turned, scanned all of us, and he issued the next order to me personally, because it had to do with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And could you please tell us: What order did Momir Nikolic give you?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: He said: "You will be assisting Colonel Jankovic today. You will report to him and receive further instructions."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who Colonel Jankovic was at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what he looked like?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know from which unit, what part of the VRS, he came from?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know any of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Nikolic provide you with any clarification as to who this Colonel Jankovic was and what role he had there in Potocari on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: He just pointed him out to me. When I asked him to show me where this Colonel Jankovic was, he turned and he pointed with his hand. Jankovic was standing maybe 20 or 30 metres away from us. He was carrying a leather bag across his shoulder. He was standing there, and I could understand that that was him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Before we get to Colonel Jankovic and your meeting with him, did Momir Nikolic explain to you his role, a role that he had been tasked, assuming one had been tasked of him?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I take it after Colonel Jankovic was pointed out to you and you having an order to go report to him, that's exactly what you did. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please tell us what happened once you reported to Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I walked up to him because, as I already pointed out, he was an officer with a rank. I introduced myself, told him my full name. I said I was a member of the military police platoon, that Momir Nikolic had sent me to report to him and to be at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what was his response?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: He just nodded and after that gave me my instructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Before you tell us what instructions you were given, could you please tell us -- in your mind at that time, could you please tell us who was your commanding officer, to your understanding.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, as I understood at that moment, and in view of the rank, it was Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please tell us what instructions or orders Colonel Jankovic gave you.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: He explained to me in broad terms what my role would be, what my assignments would be for the day, what we would be doing, what would happen, briefly what his part would be with my assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us in sort of a broad -- in broad terms what your role was.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: He explained to me that buses and trucks would arrive and that civilians were about to be driven away from Potocari to Kladanj. He said it was his assignment, in which I would assist him, to count the people coming out and he also mentioned he would ask Momir to involve more members of the military police to help us in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said that it was his assignment. Did he tell you who had given him this assignment?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were more military police officers of the Bratunac Brigade provided, as he had indicated he would be asking Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were there already. It was just a matter of engaging them for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Before we go into great details as to what you did during -- and what you saw during those two days while you were there, could you please tell us: Did you in fact carry out these tasks that were ordered to you by Colonel Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, could you please tell us, just very briefly, how long were you in Potocari carrying out this task, that is of counting how many people were going into the buses?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us how long were you there on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I spent there the whole day of the 12th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you there on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just very briefly, what did you do on the 13th in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The same tasks as the previous day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just one final question before we perhaps break for the morning: Was Colonel Jankovic there on the 13th as your commanding officer, as you understood it to be at that point in time, giving you orders with respect to this particular task?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this may be a good time then. We'll pick up from the 12th and go in detail step by step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break and we'll resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Janjic, now what I would like to do is go into detail about your activities in Potocari on July 12th, 1995, after you reported to Colonel Jankovic and you received your orders. First of all, could you please tell us: Do you recall about what time it was when you approached Colonel Jankovic and he told you what your tasks would be?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact time, but it was in the morning in any case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall whether at that point in time buses and trucks had arrived in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No. He said: "When the buses and trucks arrive," which means we were waiting for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it when you were there you were able to see the mass of people that had gathered at Potocari. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us where you were in relation to this mass of people, where you and Colonel Jankovic were standing or sitting in relation to the mass of people.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, in relation to the crowd, we were standing about 100 metres away, closer to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, at that point in time when you went to see Colonel Jankovic, did you notice whether there were any officers from the Main Staff or the corps, the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who you saw.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I saw a certain number of officers whom I didn't know at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what about later on?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It was later. I don't remember the time. I noticed General Krstic with his entourage, and I couldn't tell you whether it was at that moment or a bit later, but General Mladic with his entourage showed up and a certain number of other officers whom I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what they were doing there?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to listen in? Were you close enough to them to hear what, if anything, they were saying?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: At some point I heard General Krstic talking -- I don't know what he was saying. He was giving some sort of interview or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What about General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: He too stayed a while when he came. He was also about 100 metres away from the -- that place towards Bratunac -- I mean another hundred metres away in relation to us. He was standing with a group of officers, and they were talking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to hear from that distance what General Mladic was saying?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever learn during the course of the day what, if anything, General Mladic had said while he was in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what you learned.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As I found out, when he moved towards the checkpoint -- towards the barrier where civilians were standing, he also stayed a while at that point. And after that I heard stories from people who happened to be there at that moment, that he said to those people behind him that buses would arrive soon, that they should be patient, and that they would be transported to Kladanj or wherever they wanted to be taken, that they were safe, that there would be no problems for them. But he also asked them that women and children should leave first because they have priority, and men should wait a while longer and be patient. The heat was scorching. There were some people who were not feeling well. UNPROFOR soldiers reacted and helped them. They took some of them away to their base and brought water to others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, were you able to hear what, if anything, General Krstic had said when he was there?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just for the record I would like to show you a photograph that has been provided to us from the Office of the Prosecution. It's a still from a video. And I'm showing you what has been marked as an exhibit as P22, and I believe it's C10 V8. It's from a booklet. It has an ERN of 0291-6170. Do you recognise anyone in that photo, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who you recognise.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, under number 2, I see General Krstic, and number 1 is me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what day this would have been when you're seen in somewhat close proximity to General Krstic? Would this be the 12th or the 13th, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, meaning you don't know which of the two days?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know which day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the background can you make out what's there, from looking at the background behind you?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I see those buses. I can see that they are empty and they are probably waiting for people to get in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no further need for this photo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we can get back to your instructions with Colonel Jankovic. Now, at some point I take it buses did arrive. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you please explain to us what happened and what you did once those buses arrived.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: At the moment when the buses arrived, I took the route that I had been given earlier. It was my task to count the people getting into the buses, and I was getting ready to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the method that you used in counting the people.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said earlier, part of the other members of the military police helped in the counting. In some places two of them would stand together, such as the front door and the back door, and they counted people getting in one by one. I went inside a couple of buses, where I was unable to count people while they were getting in because it was impossible, so I had to get in. Since my colleagues knew that I was reporting the numbers directly to Colonel Jankovic, they told me the numbers they had counted. I noted all that down, and it took us an hour or two the way we were doing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please tell us how you were keeping track of these numbers.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, this first hour or two I noted down the number of people who got into each bus. I added up the numbers. And at first I reported directly to Colonel Jankovic as soon as I was done, but it was getting impossible to go back and forth after a while. So I asked Colonel Jankovic if it would be possible to operate with an average number of people that could be loaded onto one bus and then multiplied by the number of buses or trucks, and he approved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you writing these figures down?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: These numbers that I noted down I reported to him. And I was done with that. And then I started using a different method. I drew little lines for every person that got into a trailer truck, truck, or bus into a table that I had prepared earlier, based on the average number of people each vehicle could take. And then I reported those numbers to him, those tables, and he converted them into numbers because he had more time at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say you noted them down. I guess concretely, how did you note them down?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I made a diagram, a table, with columns for buses, trucks, and trailer trucks. If there were five buses, I would put five lines in the column marked "buses."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what sort of writing material for you using?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: A pen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a notebook? Did you have just loose paper? That's what I'm trying to establish at this point.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I had a ballpoint pen; all members of the military police had them. We had very small notebooks that we used in our regular military police work. And when I first reported to Colonel Jankovic, he tore a couple of sheets from that notebook that I gave him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that what you were using, the sheets of paper, to note how many people were entering the buses?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often would you report to Colonel Jankovic during the day, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but I reported several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what the final figure was for the first day that you had come up with?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: There were about 9.000 and several hundreds. I don't remember the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, aside from you and the military police of the Bratunac Brigade, was anyone else involved in this counting process?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And could you please tell us who.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: A member of the civilian police took part in the counting, too. I knew him personally. He was involved in the counting as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall what this person's name was? I'm sure the Prosecution would like to know.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Milisav Ilic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know to whom he was reporting? We know that you were reporting to Colonel Jankovic. To whom was Mr. Ilic reporting to?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I did not notice that he was reporting to anyone. I would just like to point out that from the very first moment he never entered the buses. He was only counting the buses. At one point in time he asked me for the average number of people that one bus could take, and that was about it. We didn't have any particularly frequent contacts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the members of the Bratunac Brigade that were assisting you in this process help you out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That may be leading. I don't know if there's a foundation for that question. This reference to members of the Bratunac Brigade assisting in the counting, unless that's limited to the other military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, the military --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe the question itself is not clear, especially on the members of the Bratunac Brigade. Do you mean the military police or some soldiers from the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, so far, Your Honour, we haven't heard about anybody else assisting in the counting process. I would like to point out that I haven't finished the question. And I take it I'm going to be allowed to interrupt midstream as well. But if I may be allowed to finish my question, it will become obvious that I'm referring to the military police of the Bratunac Brigade that the gentleman has already indicated in a prior session, which perhaps Mr. Shin has forgotten because he's so busy writing notes. That's what I'm referring to. Because the gentleman did indicate that others were there to assist him, and he's even testified to that just ten minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think as a rule the objection should be raised after the question is finished. You may proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the other members of the Bratunac Brigade military police that were there to assist you in counting the number of passengers entering into the buses, did they remain with you for the entire day, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Other military policemen were there, too. However, the conditions became right, in terms of this task that I was carrying out with their assistance, for them to leave, not to be engaged in this task any longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you recall about what time of the day it was when the other members of the Bratunac Brigade military police left you and you were there by yourself carrying out this task, under the direction and control of Colonel Jankovic of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I did not say that they left. They left their activities. They abandoned their activities, but some time went by. This counting took place for an hour and a half or two. I am not sure. And after that, they stopped doing what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall after they abandoned their activities what they ended up doing? Were you able to see?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please describe to us what you saw them doing.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Except for a few of them who were simply there uninterested and without any special obligations, I noticed that that vehicle had already arrived, the combat vehicle. That's what we called it. It arrived at a given point in time around noon, and part of the policemen boarded that vehicle and went somewhere. I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just a point of clarification. When you were noting the number of people getting on to the buses, were you also noting the registration of the vehicles so you could keep track of which vehicles were coming and how many were boarding the particular vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No, nobody asked me to do that and I was not given that task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were there on that particular day carrying out these activities, were you able to see whether any members of the Bratunac Brigade, whether they be military police or soldiers, were committing any abuses or atrocities toward the Muslim population that was there in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see men being separated from their families?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're sure about that?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us about what time of day it would have been or how long had you been there when you noticed these activities.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It was when these first buses were there, that first morning. We're talking about that morning when these first activities started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you please tell us: Who was engaged in this activity, that is, the separation of men from their family members?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: While we were waiting all that time for those first buses to arrive, just before they did arrive I noticed that some officers whom I did not know were issuing orders and making some kind of plan, schedule of activities, for some persons unknown to me. Throughout this time, I had personal contacts with these persons. I spoke to them. Since they were unknown persons, it is out of curiosity that we talked and we were asking each other who came from where. And of course I asked them, too, where they came from. They said to me: "We come from the specials." That was clear to me. It was an abbreviation for the special police. That was the word they used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, that -- would that be civilian police or military police?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the special police is within the ranks of the civilian police. It is a special unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Part of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us how they were dressed.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: They were not dressed the same way all of them. Some of them wore camouflage uniforms that were similar to military uniforms, our uniforms. Some of them had dark clothes, black clothes, black uniforms, even black overalls, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they ever inform you who was their commander?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No, and I didn't ask them either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask them or did they ever inform you as to who had given them the order to carry out the activities that you were able to observe them carrying out, that is the separation of the men from their families?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: When these first people came out, when the first few buses were there, at the very exit 80 or 100 metres away, I cannot be precise about that, I noticed that women and children and some old, exhausted people or men came towards me, towards the buses. I also noticed that groups of men were being taken across the street to the other side and that they moved in the direction of Bratunac. That is to say, towards me, too. I found that to be strange at that moment. I asked the policemen who were next to me why this was being done. They just explained what I had heard before, that Mladic said that that is the way it would be and that they were working in accordance with plans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you see Momir Nikolic there at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: At that time, at that moment, right over there, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in Potocari on the 12th, after he had given you your orders, ordering you, that is, to report to Colonel Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very often on several occasions, but it wasn't non-stop. It would happen every now and then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us what, if anything, Momir Nikolic was doing while he was in Potocari, that is, what you saw him doing.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No meaning what? You didn't see him doing anything?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I did not notice any special activities. For the most part, he just strolled around, came and went. I noticed that he talked to some of these officers whom I did not know. That's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was Mr. Nikolic dressed?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, how can I put it? As usual, he was showing off. He was all dressed up. That's the kind of person he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have his sunglasses on?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It was hardly ever that he did not wear them. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you notice Colonel Blagojevic, the commander of the Bratunac Brigade there, on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you were also in Potocari on the 13th. Did you notice Colonel Blagojevic on the 13th in Potocari while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to go into great detail about the 13th, but on that day did you see Momir Nikolic there by any chance?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's get back to the 12th. You said that you noticed the separation going on, and at one point I believe you indicated that the men were being taken someplace. Could you please describe to us where you noticed the men to be taken to.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were going to the other side of the street opposite the buses. So looking from Bratunac, it was the right-hand side. They were taken in the direction of Bratunac, that is to say, that was where the battery manufacturing factory was or the concrete manufacturing factory; I confuse the two. So it's on the right-hand side. There was a big building there, too. Now, was it a house or what kind of building it was, a factory, whatever, I don't know. They were brought into the yard of that particular building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether they were put into that building itself?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I could not see because I did not approach the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us from where you were standing what the distance would have been.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It's 50 metres, 80 metres, I cannot be more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you notice anything unusual about what was happening to these men or what was being done with these men?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice whether any of them -- from where you were standing, that is, if any of them were abused?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I didn't notice anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see what, if anything, was happening to their belongings?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: That, I did notice, what was going on with their personal belongings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please describe to us what you were able to observe from the 50 to 80 metres distance that you were from?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: When I would turn around, when I would look in that direction, I would see that these people who approached the gate of that building, if I can call it that, at the gate they put next to themselves all the luggage they had, rucksacks, bags, whatever they were. They would put it down by themselves, on their own. I did not see anyone issuing such orders to them. Then they would enter the compound without that luggage. They would leave the luggage by the gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you noticed this activity, what was going through your mind? Did that make an impression, and if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: My assumption was that probably these people who were taking them there were asking them for reasons of safety and security to leave that behind because perhaps somebody might have a weapon in all of that. I've already said that in addition to all of us, the general was present there, too, so I assumed that it was for reasons of safety and security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, was the general which -- we're speaking of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm referring to him, and I'm also referring to the safety and security of all of us there, policemen, officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was General Mladic there the entire day?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether these men or were you able to see -- let me put it that way. Did you observe whether these men were being frisked for weapons as they were being placed in this yard or in the building?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I didn't notice that. From the place where I was, I didn't notice any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that particular day, July 12th, 1995, did any of those men that you were able to see that had been separated and placed in that location, did any of them get on any buses to leave that area?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About what time of day did that happen? And we're speaking of July 12th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It could have been late in the afternoon, pretty late in the afternoon. I don't know what time exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we go into any great details about this activity, could you please tell us whether the men that ended up boarding the buses were also counted by you as part of the process that had been assigned to you by Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I counted their buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know or do you recall whether you kept a separate accounting of those individuals, or did you throw them into the mix with all the rest?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No, not with all the rest. All the buses were there at that moment, and I brought them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given any specific instructions by Colonel Jankovic with regards to these males, Muslim males, from Potocari, whether you should count them, and if so, whether they should be counted separately?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was given instructions. He did not ask for anything special, just at one moment he said -- because women were also boarding a bit away from the place where I was at that time. They were being boarded a bit -- at a lower point about 80 metres away. The buses were parked from that gate towards Bratunac. So there was about 10 or 15 buses times their individual lengths, so that's pretty far away. At one moment, he said: "Boarding is taking place, so go a bit further down so that you don't miss that counting." So that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did Colonel Jankovic ask for a separate counting?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did the men enter the same buses or trucks with the -- with the women and children, or was this a separate boarding process, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: The buses that arrived were parked a bit further down, not where the other buses were parked, and they boarded on their own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, were you told at that time where the men were being taken, the men that started boarding some time in the afternoon of 12 July 1995, the same men that you were counting pursuant to orders by Colonel Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know offhand approximately how many buses or trucks of men left that particular day, keeping in mind that you weren't doing a separate counting?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, if I can give a free estimate, it was only buses. I have already said that, between 10 and 15 buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please tell us: Who issued the orders, if you know, for the men to be boarded on to the buses?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to the men boarding the buses, could you please tell us what you had observed with respect to where the men were being kept. How many men were there?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know the number of people, but I did notice that detail at some point. An hour or two before the boarding, the yard was full, and the yard stretches all the way to the point where I stood. And as the yard filled starting from the gate, those people were getting rather close to me. There was the wire fence between us. I had my back to them facing the trucks across the street from me. At one point I observed that some sort of mutiny was starting. People were starting to talk loudly, some unrest was beginning. They were protesting against the fact that they were being separated. They were saying: "Why are you separating us? Why aren't you allowing us to leave with our families? Maybe you are about to kill us." Those were their words. Colonel Jankovic was standing close to me at that moment, and I could hear him when he turned to them and said that they had no reason for concern, that everything would be all right. And he said that: "As you heard," those were the words he used because he assumed they had heard the orders given before, "after your women and children have left, you would join them later. There's no reason for panicking."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you believe Colonel Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please describe to us the manner, his demeanor, when he turned and began addressing this crowd, this restless crowd as you put it, of Muslim men that had been separated.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I had the impression that he was telling the truth. He was generally a calm man, and I did not doubt the honesty of his words. I thought that he at least believed what he was saying. I didn't notice that he was keeping anything from those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you learn that day, 12 July 1995, where the men had been taken?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, where did you believe they had been taken?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, I believed they were taken where they had promised -- they had been promised to be taken, to reunite with their families. That was only normal in my view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what point in time during the day did you finish your tasks in Potocari? We're talking about the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you the precise hour, but it was late afternoon, towards dusk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before leaving Potocari, would you please tell us whether Colonel Jankovic was still there.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give him an accounting, a final accounting, of the day before leaving Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No. As I said, there was no final number. The reports or numbers came in installments, so to speak, throughout the day, and he was the one who was supposed to do the adding up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before leaving Potocari, did you receive any orders?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes. An hour, an hour and a half before they left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who issued the orders?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he issue it personally or was it through someone else such as, for instance, Mirko Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: He issued that order personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what order was it that Momir Nikolic personally issued to you an hour or so before you left Potocari on July 12th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: At one point when I was momentarily left without anything particular to do, a group of us policemen were standing together and he happened to be passing by. He stopped and he said: "When you finish up here, the assembly point is outside the police building. Don't you dare to go away." He did not stay long; he just stopped by to say that. And we did not exchange any comments after we left -- after he left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you understand that order to be?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Well, I understand him to mean that we would be given further assignments that he would give us down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, how did you get back to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: We returned in our own vehicle that had made several trips there and back. That's the usual truck we used, T-A-M.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what the lighting conditions were when you arrived back at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters right in front where the police are stationed, the military police are stationed?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: It was late in the afternoon. It was already getting dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you assembled as instructed, what instructions -- what further instructions did you receive?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: As far as I was concerned, further instructions were that the security detail from the hotel should return to the same assignment, and that's what we did, meaning the same assignment as the previous evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had been in that previous assignment, Hotel Fontana, on the evening of the 11th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Incidentally, you've told us that on the day of the 11th you worked, securing the road up in Sase mine. You came to Bratunac, you were issued an order to be at Hotel Fontana, you were there all night. Then on the 12th you were all day in Potocari, more or less. And now you're being told to go back at the Hotel Fontana. Did you sleep at all during this period?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I take it you went back to Hotel Fontana on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us and you -- could you please tell us about what time it would have been when you arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: I cannot be precise, but it was already getting dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. How did you get there?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Just as the previous evening. I was a part of people who were walking on foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what's the distance for those of us who haven't been to the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade? What's the distance between there and the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: Up to 1 kilometre, roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in walking from that -- from the Bratunac Brigade headquarters to the Hotel Fontana, does that route take you by any chance by the Vuk Karadzic -- what was known back then as the Vuk Karadzic school?

utterances.speaker: MILE JANJIC
utterances.text: No. That school is nowhere near our route.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your way to the Hotel Fontana, did you by any chance notice any buses or trucks full of Muslim men? And we're speaking about 12 July 1995.
